newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Lawyers urge US approve airline liability pacts.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers urge US approve airline liability pacts.

text.p: A key group of aviation lawyers has called on the United States to move "without delay" to approve inter-airline accords boosting compensation for injury and death of international passengers.

The International Air Transport Association (IATA) said on Monday the call was issued last week by the annual conference of the Aviation Law Association of Australia and New Zealand, which was held in Queenstown, New Zealand.
The Association said liability limits for compensation as set out in the post-World War Two Warsaw Convention applied for decades by the airline industry were "grossly inadequate and unsustainable".
These limits currently range from $75,000 in the United States to $150,000 in most of Europe and $350,000 in Australia.

Many IATA airlines have now signed two so-called Inter-Carrier Agreements -- the first on liability and the second on implementation -- replacing these limits with a pledge to pay full "compensatory damages".
The agreements also relieve the victim or his beneficiaries from the need to prove an airline was at fault in order to receive full compensation for death and injury.
A resolution passed by the lawyers meeting in Queenstown said the accords would also "obviate the need for protacted and expensive litigation" in compensation cases.

The two agreements were filed with the U.S. Department of Transportation on July 31 and with the European Commission in Brussels on August 19. If approved by both, the accords are due to go into force on November 1, IATA said.
But aviation sources said the appeal was directed to Washington because more problems were expected with approval there.

So far, 66 of IATA's some 240 members -- who include nearly 95 per cent of the world's airlines -- have signed the first inter-carrier agreement and 40 have signed the implementation accord, IATA said.
